content:
<Rep. Jamie Raskin>: I oppose this legislation, which should really be titled the Defund the Police in Dozens of American Jurisdictions Act. H.R. 5213 does nothing to protect the public. Instead, it attacks communities whose policy choices the Republican majority professes not to like by depriving them of federal public safety funding. This bill doesn't merely play politics with public safety, it harms and endangers the American people.
This bill would punish states and localities that have reformed their cash bail systems, prohibiting them from getting any funds whatsoever from the Byrne Justice Assistance Grant (Byrne JAG) program, the cornerstone of our federal public safety grant program. Byrne JAG grants supply millions of dollars of essential support to state and local police departments, prosecutors, and victim advocates across America to keep our communities safe.
Instead of targeting criminals or helping to combat crime, this bill would actually target law enforcement, erasing federal funds that officers and district attorneys need to combat, prosecute, and punish crime. And it would target crime victims who rely on the vital support that Byrne JAG funds provide.
Needlessly punitive and hopelessly vague, this legislation is apparently intended to punish jurisdictions that have enacted ``cashless bail'' for a set of covered offenses. While many jurisdictions have moved away from a system of pretrial release that relies entirely on cash bail, that is their constitutional prerogative. Half of Americans are living from paycheck to paycheck. Lots of Americans simply can't afford to put up the cash for bail--even if they pose no risk of danger to anyone else and no risk that they would flee.
We should all agree: If someone awaiting trial is a danger to the community or they are a flight risk, it shouldn't matter how much money that person has. They should be detained, period. Likewise, if someone does not pose a risk, they should not lose their liberty simply because of their poverty.
They say life is unfair but that shouldn't be the law. Some cash bail policies seem like they were pulled out of the pages of Charles Dickens: wealthy defendants can effectively buy their way out of jail while lower income people who pose no greater risk must languish behind bars indefinitely simply because they don't have the money for it. That really is out of ``A Tale of Two Cities.''
That is why some states and localities have decided that reforming, in some cases eliminating, cash bail would help reduce inequity in the criminal justice system while ensuring public safety is protected. These jurisdictions have decided for themselves that if a person is not a danger to the community, that person's freedom should not depend on whether or not they can afford to post bail.
But this legislation assumes Congress knows better than these communities do and imposes harsh penalties on their citizens that would actually make them less safe by cutting law enforcement funding in a reprisal against them for policy reasons. Congress actually requires federal courts to follow the very same pretrial release policies that would disqualify states and localities under this bill. There is no good reason to treat pretrial release from state and local courts differently than federal ones. That is what this deeply anti-local bill does.
Unfortunately, our colleagues want to play politics with public safety, but they are hurting the very people they say they want to protect--law enforcement and victims of crime.
I urge my colleagues to join me in voting no on this gross federal overreach.
Jamie Raskin,
Ranking Member.
